chunks.source: Directive 2009/128/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the sustainable use of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Product labels, buffer zones and records
chunks.heading: The label comes first
chunks.text:
Product labels, buffer zones and records — The label comes first

The product label is the legal and practical reference for application rates, crops, timing, weather limits, buffer zones and protective equipment. General guidance never overrides the label.

chunks.source: Directive 2009/128/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the sustainable use of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Product labels, buffer zones and records
chunks.heading: Buffer zones and sensitive areas
chunks.text:
Product labels, buffer zones and records — Buffer zones and sensitive areas

Labels and national rules may require untreated buffer zones next to surface water, field margins and other sensitive areas. Measures to protect the aquatic environment and drinking water are a core part of the EU framework for sustainable pesticide use.

chunks.source: Directive 2009/128/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the sustainable use of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Product labels, buffer zones and records
chunks.heading: Protective equipment and records
chunks.text:
Product labels, buffer zones and records — Protective equipment and records

Wear the personal protective equipment required by the label when mixing and spraying. Keep records of what was applied, where, when, at what rate and in which weather, as required by national rules.

chunks.source: Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products; product labels
chunks.title: Rain after application and rainfastness
chunks.heading: Rainfastness
chunks.text:
Rain after application and rainfastness — Rainfastness

The rainfast period is the time a product needs after application before rain no longer reduces its effect. It differs between products and formulations, from less than an hour to many hours, so the label is the reference.

chunks.source: Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products; product labels
chunks.title: Rain after application and rainfastness
chunks.heading: Planning around rain
chunks.text:
Rain after application and rainfastness — Planning around rain

Check the forecast for the hours after spraying, not only the current weather. If rain is likely within the rainfast period, postpone the application. Heavy rain soon after spraying also increases the risk of run-off into ditches and watercourses.

chunks.source: Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products; product labels
chunks.title: Rain after application and rainfastness
chunks.heading: Wet foliage
chunks.text:
Rain after application and rainfastness — Wet foliage

Spraying onto leaves that are already wet from rain or heavy dew can dilute the spray and make it run off the leaf. Wait until the crop has dried unless the label says otherwise.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Spray drift and how to reduce it
chunks.heading: What spray drift is
chunks.text:
Spray drift and how to reduce it — What spray drift is

Spray drift is the movement of spray droplets or vapour away from the target area during or after application. It wastes product, reduces control on the field and can damage neighbouring crops, water and wildlife.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Spray drift and how to reduce it
chunks.heading: Main factors
chunks.text:
Spray drift and how to reduce it — Main factors

Drift increases with wind speed, smaller droplet size, greater boom height, higher travel speed and higher spray pressure. Hot and dry air makes droplets evaporate and become smaller, which increases drift further.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Spray drift and how to reduce it
chunks.heading: Practical measures
chunks.text:
Spray drift and how to reduce it — Practical measures

Use low-drift nozzles where the label allows, keep the boom as low as practical for the nozzle type, avoid excessive pressure and speed, and stop spraying when conditions change. Leave untreated buffer zones next to sensitive areas as required by the label and local rules.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), spray application guidance on Delta T
chunks.title: Temperature, humidity and Delta T
chunks.heading: Evaporation of droplets
chunks.text:
Temperature, humidity and Delta T — Evaporation of droplets

In hot and dry air droplets evaporate quickly. They become smaller, drift further and may not reach the target, while very humid and cool conditions slow drying on the leaf.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), spray application guidance on Delta T
chunks.title: Temperature, humidity and Delta T
chunks.heading: Delta T
chunks.text:
Temperature, humidity and Delta T — Delta T

Delta T is the difference between the dry-bulb and wet-bulb air temperature and is a simple indicator of evaporation conditions. Values of about 2 to 8 °C are commonly described as favourable for spraying, above about 10 °C as unfavourable, and very low values can point to inversion-prone, humid conditions.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), spray application guidance on Delta T
chunks.title: Temperature, humidity and Delta T
chunks.heading: Practical use
chunks.text:
Temperature, humidity and Delta T — Practical use

When the day is getting hot and dry, spray earlier in the morning once any inversion has lifted, or later when temperature falls, and choose coarser droplets where the label allows.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), Surface temperature inversions and spraying, fact sheet
chunks.title: Temperature inversions
chunks.heading: What an inversion is
chunks.text:
Temperature inversions — What an inversion is

Normally air gets cooler with height. During a surface temperature inversion a layer of cool air lies near the ground under warmer air. This usually forms on clear, calm evenings and nights and can persist into the early morning.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), Surface temperature inversions and spraying, fact sheet
chunks.title: Temperature inversions
chunks.heading: Why it matters for spraying
chunks.text:
Temperature inversions — Why it matters for spraying

Inside an inversion small droplets can hang in the cool air layer and travel long distances sideways before settling, sometimes damaging crops far from the field. This is why spraying in dead calm conditions is discouraged.

chunks.source: GRDC (Grains Research and Development Corporation), Surface temperature inversions and spraying, fact sheet
chunks.title: Temperature inversions
chunks.heading: Signs of an inversion
chunks.text:
Temperature inversions — Signs of an inversion

Typical signs are very low wind or calm, clear skies at night or early morning, mist or fog, dew, and smoke or dust that hangs in a layer instead of rising. If these signs are present, delay spraying until the air mixes, usually after the sun has warmed the ground and a light breeze has started.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Weather conditions for spraying
chunks.heading: Wind speed
chunks.text:
Weather conditions for spraying — Wind speed

Spray in a steady, light breeze. Very strong wind carries droplets off target, and dead calm is also risky because it often comes with temperature inversions. A light breeze of roughly 1 to 4 m/s is commonly treated as the working range for boom sprayers; always follow stricter limits on the product label.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Weather conditions for spraying
chunks.heading: Wind direction
chunks.text:
Weather conditions for spraying — Wind direction

Check wind direction before and during application. Do not spray when the wind blows towards sensitive areas such as water bodies, neighbouring crops, gardens, houses or nature areas.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Weather conditions for spraying
chunks.heading: Temperature
chunks.text:
Weather conditions for spraying — Temperature

High temperatures increase evaporation of small droplets and the risk of vapour drift, and some products work poorly in cold weather. A moderate temperature range, often around 10 to 25 °C, is generally preferred; the label may set its own limits.

chunks.source: FAO (2001), Guidelines on good practice for ground application of pesticides; Defra/HSE (2006), Code of Practice for Using Plant Protection Products
chunks.title: Weather conditions for spraying
chunks.heading: Rain before and after spraying
chunks.text:
Weather conditions for spraying — Rain before and after spraying

Do not spray on wet foliage if the product needs to dry on the leaf, and avoid application when rain is expected before the product is rainfast. Rain shortly after spraying can wash the product off the crop and into watercourses.
